issues.legal_issue: The evidence established beyond reasonable doubt that the accused identified as the shooter committed the murder, despite challenges concerning the medical evidence, firearm recovery, identification, and the first report.
material_facts: Two eyewitnesses testified that the accused fired three shots at the deceased, and their testimony remained credible after cross-examination.

The medical evidence recorded oval wounds and a downward, right-to-left path of the pellets, which the court found consistent with shots fired from an elevated position; the doctor could not give a clear opinion on firing distance.

The prosecution established the place of occurrence through recovered pellets and blood-stained earth, and the court found that the recovery of a second firearm did not undermine the evidence identifying the gun used.
The witnesses testified that it was a moonlit night, a lantern was burning, and they knew the accused and his voice and appearance.
The first report was lodged by a village watchman who was not an eyewitness, after the deceased’s father asked him to report the occurrence.
issues.conclusion: The prosecution proved beyond reasonable doubt that the accused identified as the shooter committed the murder, and his conviction and sentence were maintained.
issues.legal_principle: A court must assess the totality of the evidence and make a genuine effort to ascertain the truth; a variance between eyewitness testimony and medical evidence does not automatically require rejection of the prosecution case. Credible eyewitness testimony may prevail over an expert opinion on firing distance (Karnail Singh v. State of Punjab, AIR 1971 SC 2119). The discussion of Taylor’s Principles and Practice of Medical Jurisprudence, Modi’s Medical Jurisprudence and Toxicology, and Shiv Shankar v. State, AIR 1953 All. 652, supports the conclusion that blackening around a wound does not invariably establish close-range firing. The court also relied on the circumstances of identification, the corroborative medical features, the scene evidence, and the fact that a first report lodged by a non-eyewitness need not contain detailed accounts of each person’s role.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_from_conviction and credible_eyewitnesses and medical_features_corrob_shooter_account and scene_and_weapon_corroboration and favorable_identification_conditions and first_report_made_by_nonwitness

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_conviction: The proceeding is a criminal appeal challenging a conviction.
predicates.credible_eyewitnesses: Two eyewitnesses who were present described the accused firing at the deceased, and their testimony remained credible under cross-examination.
predicates.medical_features_corrob_shooter_account: The shape and direction of the injuries were consistent with the eyewitness account of shots fired from an elevated position.
predicates.scene_and_weapon_corroboration: Physical evidence at the scene and the firearm evidence supported the account of the shooting.
predicates.favorable_identification_conditions: The witnesses had adequate light to see the accused and already knew their appearance and voices.
predicates.first_report_made_by_nonwitness: A person who did not witness the crime lodged the first report after receiving information from a witness.

issues.definition: When a criminal appeal challenges a conviction, credible eyewitness testimony supported by the medical and other circumstances can sustain the shooter’s conviction even when the first report was lodged by a non-eyewitness.

issues.legal_issue: The evidence did not establish beyond reasonable doubt that an accused who played no active role and made only a late, ambiguous exhortation shared the shooter’s intention to kill.
material_facts: The occurrence developed during a spontaneous altercation and was not a planned killing.
The accused who fired had threatened and abused the deceased before the other accused’s father exhorted him to kill.
The accused whose liability was at issue was attributed only a final exhortation that could mean either to kill or to beat the deceased.
No other active role was attributed to that accused, and the evidence did not establish that his intention to share the killing had formed before the shooting.
issues.conclusion: The prosecution did not prove beyond reasonable doubt that the accused shared the common intention to kill; his conviction was set aside and he was to be released unless required in connection with another offence.
issues.legal_principle: For liability based on common intention under Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code, the prosecution must prove that the accused shared the relevant intention. Common intention may develop during an occurrence, but the sequence of events, the accused’s conduct, and the nature and timing of any exhortation must establish that shared intention beyond reasonable doubt. A late and ambiguous exhortation, without more, was insufficient on these facts.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_from_conviction and spontaneous_occurrence and primary_actor_intent_preceded_accused_role and only_late_ambiguous_exhortation and no_other_active_role

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_conviction: The proceeding is a criminal appeal challenging a conviction based on alleged participation in a shared criminal intention.
predicates.spontaneous_occurrence: The criminal event arose from an altercation rather than a preplanned design.
predicates.primary_actor_intent_preceded_accused_ro: The person who committed the principal act had already expressed an intention to kill before the accused’s alleged contribution.
predicates.only_late_ambiguous_exhortation: The accused was attributed only a late exhortation whose words could be understood as urging either killing or beating.
predicates.no_other_active_role: The evidence attributed no other active participation in the crime to the accused.

issues.definition: When a spontaneous occurrence involves an already expressed intention by the principal actor, and another accused contributes only a late ambiguous exhortation without any other active role, shared intention is not proved.
